problem: The cost factor is called '10 to 12 rounds'. In bcrypt the cost is a logarithmic work factor: cost 10 means 2^10 ≈ 1024 key-setup iterations, and each extra unit doubles the time. A student can read this as 'only 10 to 12 passes over the password'.
fix: Write: 'bcrypt takes a cost factor, usually 10 to 12; the cost is an exponent, so cost 12 does 2^12 ≈ 4096 iterations, four times the work of cost 10.'

problem: The verification step is incomplete. The server must also check that the header's alg value is the expected one and reject alg 'none'; verifying only the signature and exp leaves the classic 'alg: none' forgery open. The text also implies the key is always one secret; with RS256/ES256 the server signs with a private key and others verify with the public key.
fix: Add: 'Verify the token with the expected algorithm only, and reject tokens whose header says alg none or any algorithm you did not choose. With HMAC the same secret signs and verifies; with RSA or ECDSA the server signs with a private key and any service verifies with the public key.'

problem: 'SameSite=Lax or Strict stops another site from making the browser send the cookie on a cross-site request' overstates Lax. Lax still sends the cookie on top-level cross-site GET navigations; it blocks cross-site POST, fetch and form submissions.
fix: Write: 'SameSite=Strict sends the cookie only on same-site requests. Lax still sends it on top-level cross-site GET navigations but blocks cross-site POST, fetch and form posts. Either one reduces CSRF, and Lax is the common default.'

problem: 'Keep it in memory or in an HttpOnly cookie' is given without the catch: an HttpOnly cookie is sent automatically by the browser, so CSRF protection (SameSite, CSRF token) becomes necessary, and the Authorization: Bearer pattern no longer applies.
fix: Add: 'If you keep the JWT in an HttpOnly cookie, the browser sends it automatically, so set SameSite and add a CSRF token; the Authorization: Bearer header is used only when the code holds the token in memory.'
